title: Episode 122: Andrew Jackson and the Battle of New Orleans: The Miracle on the Mississippi
description:
In December eighteen fourteen, during the waning months of the War of eighteen-twelve, Great Britain launched its most formidable offensive of the conflict. Fresh from their victory over Napoleon in Europe, a royal fleet carrying ten thousand veteran soldiers—the conquerors of Spain and France—anchored in the Gulf of Mexico under Major General Sir Edward Pakenham. Their objective was total: capture New Orleans, seize control of the mouth of the Mississippi River, and sever the American interior from the Atlantic seaboard.

Standing against this juggernaut was Major General Andrew Jackson, 'Old Hickory,' an iron-willed frontier soldier wasted by dysentery and carrying British bullet lead in his chest from past duels. With fewer than five thousand men, Jackson assembled the most improbable, diverse coalition in American military history: Tennessee and Kentucky backwoods sharpshooters, wealthy New Orleans Creoles, free Black militia battalions, Choctaw warriors, federal marines, and the notorious smugglers and cannons of Jean Lafitte's Baratarian pirate fleet.

Digging deep trenches and throwing up mud-and-cotton ramparts along the Rodriguez Canal on the Chalmette plains, Jackson waited. On the freezing, fog-drenched morning of January eighth, eighteen fifteen, Pakenham ordered a direct frontal assault. In less than thirty minutes of devastating artillery and rifle fire, Jackson's army shattered the pride of the British Empire, losing only thirteen men while inflicting over two thousand casualties. Here is the legendary story of the battle that catapulted Andrew Jackson into history.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the fiery world of America's seventh President, Andrew Jackson. Long before he transformed the presidency and challenged the American political establishment, Jackson was the iron-willed hero of the western frontier. In January eighteen hundred and fifteen, with the capital in ashes and the young republic reeling, Jackson stood in the swamps of Louisiana to defend New Orleans against Britain's finest army. With a ragtag band of frontiersmen, free men of color, and pirates, he achieved one of the most stunning military upsets in human history. Here is George with the Battle of New Orleans.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE PRIZE ON THE MISSISSIPPI
In the late autumn of eighteen fourteen, the British Empire moved to deliver a knockout blow to the United States. With Napoleon defeated and safely exiled to Elba, Great Britain could deploy its vast, unmatched military machine against its former colonies. A formidable armada of more than fifty royal warships carrying ten thousand elite infantry under Admiral Sir Alexander Cochrane sailed toward the Gulf of Mexico. These were not raw recruits; they were the legendary 'Wellington's Invincibles'—veteran regiments like the Ninety-Third Highlanders and the Forty-Fourth Foot who had chased French imperial legions across Spain and Portugal.
Their target was the jewel of the Gulf Coast: New Orleans. Strategically, New Orleans was the key to the entire North American continent. Situated at the mouth of the Mississippi River, it was the sole commercial outlet for the vast territories between the Appalachians and the Rocky Mountains. Whoever controlled New Orleans controlled the commerce, the food supply, and the economic destiny of the American West. British commanders privately intended to ignore the Louisiana Purchase entirely, regarding the territory as Spanish property illegally sold by Napoleon, and planned to annex the entire Mississippi Valley to the British Crown.
To defend this vital prize, the United States turned to Major General Andrew Jackson of the Tennessee militia. Known as 'Old Hickory' for his tough, unbending discipline, Jackson arrived in New Orleans in early December eighteen fourteen. He was emaciated from chronic dysentery, wracked with fever, and still carried a bullet lodged dangerously close to his heart from an eighteen-six duel. But behind his sunken eyes burned a fierce, incandescent hatred of the British Empire, dating back to his childhood in the Revolutionary War when a British officer had slashed his face with a saber for refusing to clean his boots.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: AN UNLIKELY BROTHERHOOD OF ARMS
When Jackson surveyed his defensive resources in New Orleans, the situation seemed hopeless. The city's population of French Creoles, Spanish merchants, and Anglo-Americans was divided, terrified, and rife with rumors of surrender. Jackson immediately declared martial law, suspended the civil legislature, and began assembling an army unlike anything ever seen under the American flag.
From the wilderness of Tennessee and Kentucky came three thousand backwoods riflemen, clad in homespun hunting shirts and coonskin caps, carrying long-barreled Deckard rifles capable of driving a bullet through a silver dollar at one hundred yards. Jackson recruited two battalions of free men of color—free Black citizens, French-speaking artisans, and Haitian emigres—promising them equal pay and equal bounty lands, making them the first Black units to serve under federal command since the Revolution. He added a contingent of sixty Choctaw warriors under Chief Pushmataha, along with a handful of federal infantry and marines.
Yet Jackson desperately lacked heavy artillery, naval gunners, and gunpowder. For these, Jackson made an audacious pact with the devil. Operating out of the misty bayous of Barataria Bay was a privateering and smuggling empire led by the dashing, notorious French pirate Jean Lafitte. The British had offered Lafitte thirty thousand pounds sterling and a captain's commission in the Royal Navy to guide their invasion fleet through the bayous. Lafitte spurned the British bribe and offered his men, thirty-six heavy brass naval cannons, and seven thousand pounds of premium gunpowder to Jackson in exchange for presidential pardons. Jackson shook Lafitte's hand, integrating the pirates into the line as his premier artillery crews.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE NIGHT ATTACK AND LINE JACKSON
On December twenty-third, eighteen fourteen, the British vanguard under Major General John Keane pulled off a daring amphibious landing, navigating shallow bayous to emerge at the Villeré plantation on the east bank of the Mississippi, just nine miles below New Orleans. A breathless courier dashed into Jackson's headquarters at three o'clock with the news. Jackson slammed his fist onto the table and swore: 'By the Eternal, they shall not sleep on our soil!'
Rather than waiting to be attacked, Jackson struck instantly. That night, under cover of dense fog and pitch darkness, Jackson launched a ferocious surprise assault while the American schooner Carolina bombarded the British camp from the river. In the swirling, terrifying melee of hand-to-hand combat fought with hunting knives, tomahawks, and bayonets, Jackson inflicted nearly three hundred casualties before withdrawing. The night attack did not defeat the British, but it achieved something far more vital: it stunned British commanders into cautious delay, giving Jackson four precious days to fortify a defensive position.
Jackson selected a narrow choke point between the Mississippi River on the right and an impassable cypress swamp on the left, along the line of an old, abandoned mill race known as the Rodriguez Canal. For four days and nights, Jackson's men worked frantically with shovels, picks, and cypress logs, digging the canal ten feet wide and throwing up a towering earthen parapet four feet high. Mounted along this 'Line Jackson' were sixteen heavy artillery pieces manned by Lafitte's pirates, federal naval gunners, and Louisiana Creoles.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: SIR EDWARD PAKENHAM'S GRAND PLAN
On Christmas Day, the overall British commander arrived at the front: Major General Sir Edward Pakenham. Pakenham was a thirty-six-year-old aristocratic war hero, the brother-in-law of the Duke of Wellington, celebrated for his brilliant cavalry charges at the Battle of Salamanca. But Pakenham found his army miserable, shivering in waterlogged sugarcane fields, pounded daily by American naval guns, and constantly harassed by Kentucky snipers who crept through the weeds at night to pick off British sentries.
After an intense artillery duel on New Year's Day proved that American guns could outshoot the Royal Artillery, Pakenham decided upon a classic, overwhelming European frontal assault. His plan for January eighth was ambitious. A secondary force of fourteen hundred troops under Colonel William Thornton would cross the Mississippi in boats to capture the American artillery batteries on the west bank, turning those guns to rake Jackson's line from the flank.
Simultaneously, Pakenham's main army of sixty-five hundred veterans would advance across the open Chalmette plains in two massive assault columns. Major General Samuel Gibbs would lead three thousand men against the American left near the swamp, while Major General John Keane attacked the right near the river. In the center stood the reserve: the legendary Ninety-Third Sutherland Highlanders, a towering battalion of eleven hundred giant Scotsmen clad in tartan kilts and feather bonnets. Pakenham was supremely confident that the raw American backwoodsmen would break and run the moment they saw British bayonets emerging from the mist.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE FOG LIFTS ON THE PLAINS OF CHALMETTE
Before dawn on Sunday, January eighth, eighteen fifteen, a freezing, bone-chilling mist blanketed the fields of Chalmette. Behind their earthen parapet, Jackson's men stood shoulder-to-shoulder, shivering in the dark. Jackson walked the entire length of the ramparts, inspecting the powder horns, checking the cannon fuses, and reminding his men: 'Keep cool, aim low, and see that almost every shot tells.'
At six o'clock in the morning, a British signal rocket screamed into the sky, bursting in a shower of red sparks above the swamp. Instantly, British drums rolled and bugles sounded the advance. The main British columns stepped off in magnificent, locked parade-ground formation, their scarlet coats gleaming and their thousands of bayonets leveled like a hedge of steel.
Then, disaster struck the British vanguard. The Forty-Fourth Regiment of Foot, assigned to carry the heavy scaling ladders and fascines of sugarcane to bridge the canal, had forgotten their equipment in the rear. By the time they hurried back to retrieve them, the column had advanced five hundred yards into the open plain without any means to cross the ditch or climb the American ramparts.
Suddenly, as the morning sun crested the horizon, a sharp river breeze swept across the plain, rolling away the fog like a theater curtain. There, fully exposed in broad daylight just four hundred yards away, stood the pride of the British Empire. Jackson calmly mounted the parapet and called out to his pirate gunner, Dominique You: 'Lieutenant, you have the range. Let them have it!' Dominique You blew on his match and touched the touchhole. The great thirty-two-pound brass cannon roared, tearing a massive hole through the British ranks. It was the signal for the entire American line to open fire.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THIRTY MINUTES OF DESTRUCTION
What followed was not a battle; it was a localized apocalypse. Sixteen American cannons, loaded to their muzzles with musket balls, iron scrap, and grape shot, fired continuously in deafening salvos. Simultaneously, Jackson had organized his Tennessee and Kentucky riflemen four ranks deep. The first rank stepped up to the parapet, rested their heavy rifles on cypress logs, picked their targets, and fired. As they stepped back to reload, the second rank stepped up and fired, followed by the third and fourth, creating a rolling, unbroken sheet of flame and lead.
The British soldiers walked straight into an inescapable wall of metal. Entire platoons were swept away in single volleys. Officers were targeted with ruthless precision; within ten minutes, virtually every British colonel, major, and captain in the assault columns was killed or wounded. General Gibbs fell mortally wounded twenty yards from the canal. Seeing his army disintegrating into panic, Sir Edward Pakenham rode gallantly to the front of the line, waving his hat to rally the men. His horse was shot dead beneath him, and as he mounted a second horse, grape shot shattered his right arm. Moments later, another volley tore through his thigh and spine, mortally wounding the British commander-in-chief.
In a desperate effort to restore order, the Ninety-Third Highlanders marched forward into the killing ground, their bagpipes skirling above the roar of cannon. But without orders to advance or retreat, the brave Scotsmen halted eighty yards from the ramparts, standing erect in dress formation under continuous rifle fire. Hundreds were cut down where they stood. In less than thirty minutes, the British army was utterly shattered, fleeing in wild disorder toward the swamp.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE MYTH OF OLD HICKORY AND A NATION'S REBIRTH
When the smoke cleared from the Chalmette plain, a scene of unimaginable slaughter was revealed. More than two thousand British soldiers lay killed, wounded, or captured, including three major generals and eight senior commanders. Pakenham's body was recovered, placed in a cask of rum to preserve it, and shipped home to England.
Behind Line Jackson, the American casualties were miraculous: only thirteen men killed and thirty-nine wounded. Never in modern military history had an invading superpower suffered so lopsided a defeat at the hands of a citizen militia.
Ironically, two weeks before the battle, American and British diplomats in Ghent, Belgium, had signed a peace treaty ending the war. Because news took weeks to cross the winter Atlantic by sailing ship, neither Jackson nor Pakenham knew the treaty existed. Critics later claimed the battle was fought in vain. But historians know better: had the British captured New Orleans, they would have occupied the mouth of the Mississippi and likely refused to surrender the Louisiana territory, contesting the validity of the purchase. Jackson's victory secured the continental destiny of the United States forever.
When news of New Orleans reached Washington, it detonated a wave of ecstatic, euphoric patriotism. The shame of the burning Capitol was wiped away overnight. Andrew Jackson became the towering living hero of the republic, the symbol of the unconquerable American common man. The road that began in the blood and fog of the Rodriguez Canal would lead 'Old Hickory' straight to the White House, forever changing the course of American democracy.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Battle of New Orleans transformed Andrew Jackson from a frontier general into a legendary national icon. It showed the world that a free, diverse citizen army could defeat the greatest professional military on Earth. Next week, we explore Andrew Jackson's greatest domestic trial as President: the Nullification Crisis of eighteen hundred and thirty-two, where he stood toe-to-toe with his own Vice President, John C. Calhoun, threatening to hang any man who dared commit treason against the United States. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
